title: Re-creating Original New York Times Graphic visualization
text:
What the Visualization contains

Temperature graph

Bands for the record, normal, and actual highs and lows are shown in the correct colors.
Downward triangles point to the record high temperatures above the red band.
Text displays the record high temperatures above the triangles.
X-axis label: 3-letter month abbreviations appear in the middle of each month.
Y-axis label: Tick marks at 0, 40, 80, and 120 only.
Vertical lines separate the months.
Title of “Temperature” is included.


Precipitation

Tan area and blue line reflecting the monthly cumulative precipitation is included.
Text (number) for cumulative precipitation for each month is included at the end of each month just above the blue line.
Downward triangles point to the record precipitation days.
Vertical lines separate the months.
Title of “Precipitation” is included.


Overall

Both the temperature and precipitation graphs are in one figure.
The temperature plot takes up more vertical space than the precipitation plot.
The title “SFO weather in 2011” is present.

Setup

Code# Code for loading packages and reading in data
library(tidyverse)
weather <- read_csv("https://mac-stat.github.io/data/sfo_weather.csv")
head(weather)
## # A tibble: 6 × 19
##   Month   Day   Low  High NormalLow NormalHigh RecordLow LowYr RecordHigh HiYear
##   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>      <dbl>     <dbl> <dbl>      <dbl>  <dbl>
## 1     1     1    47    52        44         56        31  1965         68   1996
## 2     1     2    48    51        44         56        29  1960         69   1996
## 3     1     3    45    53        44         56        31  1950         69   2000
## 4     1     4    39    53        44         56        29  1949         62   2006
## 5     1     5    38    55        44         56        26  1949         65   1986
## 6     1     6    37    52        44         56        29  1950         66   2003
## # ℹ 9 more variables: Precip <dbl>, RecordPrecip <dbl>, PrecipYr <dbl>,

title: Re-creating Original New York Times Graphic visualization
text:
Visualization
Creating the basic plot

Code# geom_linerange basically allows to plot range data (two values of y: low and max with 1 x value )
basic_plt <-ggplot(weather, aes(x = dateInYear, ymin = weather$RecordLow, ymax = weather$RecordHigh)) + 
          geom_linerange(color = "#ECEBE3")+ scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 120), breaks = c(0, 40, 80, 120)) +         theme_classic() 

basic_plt







Adding normal and weather lows and highs

Code# to add new layer representing more y values, we just use + and continue adding layers (no seperate operator in ggplot). 
# adding new layers of normal and record lows
# just add + to add layers on saved basic plt, no need to pipe as we are just adding layers not saying "and then"

normal_record_plt <-basic_plt +
  geom_linerange(color ="#C8B8BA", aes(ymin = weather$NormalLow, ymax = weather$NormalHigh)) +
  geom_linerange(color = "#A90248", alpha = 1,  aes(ymin = weather$Low, ymax = weather$High )) + 
  labs(subtitle = "Temperature", x = " ", title = "SFO Weather in 2011" ) +  theme(plot.title =  element_text(hjust = 0.5))

normal_record_plt







Adding downward facing triangles and dotted lines

Codelibrary(ggrepel) # for repelling overlap in geom_text 


# filtering rows which whose record is True
rec_filtered <-weather %>% 
  filter(Record == TRUE)


# adding the months and dashed lines 
# to create the month lines, calculating the mid-points so that the month labels in x axis are in the middle
month_start_dates <- c(1,32, 60, 91, 121, 152, 182, 213, 244, 274, 305, 335) 
midpoints <- (month_start_dates[-length(month_start_dates)] + month_start_dates[-1]) / 2 # 
month_centers <-c( 16.5, 46.0, 75.5, 106.0, 136.0, 167.0, 197.5, 228.5, 259.0, 289.5, 320.0, 350)

 

# Adding black downward facing triangles and text on plot 
# Used the inherit.aes= False argument so that it geom_text does not inherit previous mappings(error resolved)
 achieved_plt<- normal_record_plt + 
  geom_point(data = rec_filtered, aes(x = rec_filtered$dateInYear, y = rec_filtered$RecordHigh), shape =25,fill = "black", inherit.aes = FALSE) +
   geom_text_repel(
    data = rec_filtered,
    aes(x = dateInYear, y = RecordHigh, label = RecordText),size = 1.5, inherit.aes = FALSE ) + 
    geom_vline(xintercept = month_start_dates, color = "lightgrey", linetype = "dotted", size = 0.3)+
    scale_x_continuous(labels = month.abb, breaks = month_centers, expand = c(0,0)) + labs( subtitle =              "Precipitation", x = " ", y = " ")

 

 

 # remocing the x-axis line
  achieved_plt<- achieved_plt + 
   theme(axis.line.x = element_blank())
  
  achieved_plt







Creatting the precipitation plot

Code# precipitation plot 
# triangles area, using geom_area, for blue lines using geom_line, taking only subset of weather data only takes it when record is 1 meaning it makes a record, taking a shape and, color and size
# geom_text directly puts label on the graph -- very cool! 


# Month start dates to draw dotted lines and calculating midpoints to center Months
  month_start_dates <- c(1,32, 60, 91, 121, 152, 182, 213, 244, 274, 305, 335) 
  month_centers <-c( 16.5, 46.0, 75.5, 106.0, 136.0, 167.0, 197.5, 228.5, 259.0, 289.5, 320.0, 350) 
  
# Filtering out Cumulative precipitation for the end of month dates 
  target_dates <- as.Date(c(
  "2011-01-31","2011-02-28","2011-03-31","2011-04-30","2011-05-31",
  "2011-06-30","2011-07-31","2011-08-31","2011-09-30","2011-10-31",
  "2011-11-30","2011-12-31"
))

  # Creating the column cuml_end_month 
weather <- weather %>%
  mutate(cuml_end_month = ifelse(date %in% target_dates, CulmPrec, NA))


# Creating the precipitation plot 
 precip_plt <- ggplot(weather, aes(x= dateInYear, y = CulmPrec)) + theme_classic() +
  geom_area(fill = "#ebeae2") + 
  geom_line(color = "#32a3d8") + 
  geom_point(data = subset(weather, RecordP == 1),
  shape = 25, fill = "black", size = 1.5) + scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 8), breaks = c(4,8)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept =  month_start_dates, color = "lightgray")+
  scale_x_continuous(labels = month.abb, breaks = month_centers, expand = c(0,0)) + labs( subtitle = "Precipitation", x = " ", y = " ") +    
   geom_text_repel(
    data = weather,
    aes(x = dateInYear, y = CulmPrec,label = cuml_end_month  ), size = 2, inherit.aes = FALSE ) + 
    labs(x = "", y = "") 
 
 
 # removing the x-axis line 
  precip_plt<-precip_plt +
  theme(axis.line.x = element_blank())
  precip_plt







Arranging both plots together

Code# Arranging both plts 
library(gridExtra)
plot1 <-achieved_plt
plot2 <-precip_plt

grid.arrange(plot1, plot2, heights = c(11, 7.5))

It was definitely big learning in terms of plotting exact downward triangles, to drawing dotted lines after, centering Months after calculating mid-points and most importatnt solving erorrs of geom_text(). So, building the plot step by step helpmed me learn algorithmic thinking.

title: Predicting song popularity based acoustic properties
text:
Brief Introduction and Data
What makes a song popular? Can we predict popularity using only acoustic properties (eg: how fast and loud a song is)? In this I’ll analyze 247 songs that play on Spotify. Along with the popularity of each song, the data contains lots of acoustic variables. To learn more about the acoustic variables, and check out the original source on Tidy Tuesday, click below
Click here
crumbs: 2  Predicting song popularity based acoustic properties

title: Predicting song popularity based acoustic properties
text:
Client Requirement
Let’s say, an executive from a Big Music streamline Company (Ex: Spotify) asks us to build a predictive model of popularity using the available set of predictors in music_sub curated dataset. They don’t have a data team, hence prefer a simpler model.
crumbs: 2  Predicting song popularity based acoustic properties

title: Predicting song popularity based acoustic properties
text:
Very brief simplified Steps

Building the Least Absolute Square Shrinkage Operator (LASSO) Model based on LASSO algorithm (L1 Linearization technique) and estimating 100 models using lambda values in range from 10^(-5) to 10^(-0.1)
Getting the best penalty and most parsimonious penalty from our most accurate model (aka Least Squares, lambda = 0 ) and most parsimonious model (Final Lasso model)
Fitting final lasso model and creating the equation ; 7 predictors penalized ; and calculating cv mae difference lasso model and least squares model
Justifying the reasonability of the parsimonious model through rule of thumb (mae within +-1 standard deviation ) to tackle the goldilocks problem
Plotting the lambda vs coefficients plot to understand strongest predictors and also re-assure that lambda chose for my LASSO is reasonable – does not penalize too much or too little
Finalizing my LASSO model by testing my prediction by againt least square Model’s prediction and seeing if it falls with the range; proving it’s accurate based on 1 standard deviation range and also justifying why it’s computationally, economically and manually much more simpler yet super effective.
Providing my simple Recommendations to the Execeutive based on the model

title: Predicting song popularity based acoustic properties
text:
Setup

library(ggridges)

section: 1: preparing & acquainting oruselves with the data
text:
1: preparing & acquainting oruselves with the data
Part a

Code# range of popularity of outcomes using the range function

range(music$popularity)
## [1] 21 98


Minimum = 21 , Maximum = 98
Part b

Code# Selecting just 3 cloumns and top 6 head(6)
most_pop_6 <- music %>% 
  select(artist, title, popularity) %>% 
  head(6)


Part c

Code# joy plot 
ggplot(music, aes(x = popularity, y = artist)) +
  geom_density_ridges() + 
  theme_ridges() 







I don’t know any artist, but Post Malone seems to have highest popularity scores of 98 and seems to have two peaks indicating I think two small groups of songs which are hit. On the other hand Logic and Upchurch seems to have highest peaks relative to others even though there popularity scores are less than Post Malone showing there few groups of songs were really hit.
Part d

Code# creating the music sub data set -- removing title, album name, album release, mode, artist as we won't use them as predictors as our main focus is acoustics aesthetic

music_sub <- music %>% 
  select(popularity, genre, danceability, energy, loudness, speechiness, acousticness, instrumentalness, liveness, valence, tempo, duration_ms)
crumbs: 2  Predicting song popularity based acoustic properties

title: Predicting song popularity based acoustic properties
text:
2: LASSO (part 1)
Lasso Algorithm : Identify the model coefficients Beta 1, Beta 2, …. Beta p that minimize the penalized residual sum of squares:


where:

residual sum of squares (RSS) measures the overall model prediction error
the penalty term measures the overall size of the model coefficients
(“lambda”) is a tuning hyperparameter





Lasso Algorith

Part a

Code# Building the LASSO model

# 1. LASSO algo specification
lasso_spec <- linear_reg() %>%             
  set_mode("regression") %>% 
  set_engine("glmnet") %>%                 
  set_args(mixture = 1, penalty = tune())  



Code# 2. Variable Recipe 
variable_recipe <- recipe(popularity ~ ., data = music_sub) %>%  # the . means basically use all variables to predict popularity
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors())



Code# 3. workflow specification (model + recipe)
lasso_workflow <- workflow() %>% 
  add_recipe(variable_recipe) %>% 
  add_model(lasso_spec)



Code# 4. Estimating 100 models using lambda values in range  from 10^(-5) to 10^(-0.1
set.seed(253)
lasso_models <- lasso_workflow %>% 
  tune_grid(
    grid = grid_regular(penalty(range = c(-5, -0.1)), levels = 100),  # 100 possible values
    resamples = vfold_cv(music_sub, v = 10),   
    metrics = metric_set(mae)
  )



Code# plotting lambda vs mae 
autoplot(lasso_models) + 
  scale_x_continuous() + 
  xlab(expression(lambda))








Code# Finding the lambda which produces smallest cv mae
best_penalty <- lasso_models %>% 
  select_best(metric = "mae")

best_penalty
## # A tibble: 1 × 2
##   penalty .config          
##     <dbl> <chr>            
## 1 0.00001 pre0_mod001_post0


The lambda value producing smallest cv mae : 0.00001, basically close to 0. — This is the most accurate model producing least cv mae

Code# looking at the most parsimonious model 
autoplot(lasso_models) + 
  scale_x_continuous() + 
  xlab(expression(lambda)) + 
  geom_errorbar(data = collect_metrics(lasso_models),
                aes(x = penalty, ymin = mean - std_err, ymax = mean + std_err), 
                alpha = 0.5)








Code# getting the parsimonious lambda 

parsimonious_penalty <- lasso_models %>% 
  select_by_one_std_err(metric = "mae", desc(penalty))

parsimonious_penalty
## # A tibble: 1 × 2
##   penalty .config          
##     <dbl> <chr>            
## 1   0.794 pre0_mod100_post0


Parsimonious lambda = 0.7943282

Code# fitting the final model
final_lasso <- lasso_workflow %>% 
  finalize_workflow(parameters = parsimonious_penalty) %>% 
  fit(data = music_sub) %>% 
  tidy() %>% 
  filter(estimate != 0)

final_lasso
## # A tibble: 8 × 3
##   term             estimate penalty
##   <chr>               <dbl>   <dbl>
## 1 (Intercept)        47.0     0.794
## 2 danceability       17.4     0.794
## 3 energy             -7.68    0.794
## 4 loudness            0.193   0.794
## 5 speechiness         5.10    0.794
## 6 instrumentalness   -0.208   0.794
## 7 genre_pop          11.7     0.794
## 8 genre_rap           0.176   0.794

final_lasso_model<- lasso_workflow %>% 
  finalize_workflow(parameters = parsimonious_penalty) %>% 
  fit(data = music_sub)

final_lasso
## # A tibble: 8 × 3
##   term             estimate penalty
##   <chr>               <dbl>   <dbl>
## 1 (Intercept)        47.0     0.794
## 2 danceability       17.4     0.794
## 3 energy             -7.68    0.794
## 4 loudness            0.193   0.794
## 5 speechiness         5.10    0.794
## 6 instrumentalness   -0.208   0.794
## 7 genre_pop          11.7     0.794
## 8 genre_rap           0.176   0.794


My final model as of, I think is the parsimonious model as I think its much simpler model with 7 variables, and it has penalized 7 other variables including genre category and excluding refrence category (Since the data team is also small, we are looking for simpler model). Although, I will want to investigate more to see how accurate we want to be instead of simpler, so based on the trade-off I think I would finalize later. But as of now, my final lasso model is based on the intercept and these coefficients :
Final Lasso Model


Final Lasso Model

Part b
Exact value of lambda used in my final LASSO model is : 0.7943282
Part c
Only 6 of the original predictors remain and others have been penalized. The 6 remaining from original are : danceability, energy, loudness, speechiness, instrumentalness, and genre (pop and rap).
Part d
For my final model, the CV MAE is approximately 12.40 for lambda 0.7943282. The lowest CV MAE at 0 lambda basically least regression square is approximately 12.15. In context of our popularity scores, if we compare my LASSO model is approximately 10.3% off (12.4/120* 100) and least regression square/most accuarte model is off by 0.20, which on a 0-120 scale is insignificant. I think the difference us pretty small.
crumbs: 2  Predicting song popularity based acoustic properties

title: Predicting song popularity based acoustic properties
text:
3: LASSO (part 2)
Part a

Code# plotting lambda vs cv mae
autoplot(lasso_models) + 
  scale_x_continuous() + 
  xlab(expression(lambda)) + 
  geom_errorbar(data = collect_metrics(lasso_models),
                aes(x = penalty, ymin = mean - std_err, ymax = mean + std_err), 
                alpha = 0.5)







I think the parsimonious lambda that I got is approximately 0.8, which definitely penalized many variables and gave us a simple model and the difference between mae’s of Lasso and least square is 12.46-12.16, which is not much relative to the scale. So, I think 0.79 lambda is most parsimonious model R chose as 0.79 is still in the +- 1 standard deveation and seems perfectly reasonable. I find it reasonable based on error bars and also it fall withing 1 standard deviation.
Part b
From this plot, the clear theme to me how Lasso cv mae changes to penalty(lambda). As the penalty increase so does the Lasso cv mae. So we get most accurate model at lambda 0 and as lambda increases, the more inaccurate it becomes becomes the mae increase but large lambda also gives us a simple model. So it’s the goldilock’s problem we discussed in the class. So, balance the trade off between accuracy and simplicity, so that simpler model is not significantly worse than the best accurate model. And in our case, we were able to utilize the +- 1 standard deviation rule to get most parsimonious model, which is simple but also is not significantly worse than most accurate model. Since difference between our most parsimonious model and least squares is 12.46-12.16, is 0.20 which is pretty insignificant, and is 0.2% off on a scale of 0-120 in predicting the popularity of a song.
Part c

Code# plotting the lambda vs coefficients relationship 

all_lassos <- final_lasso_model %>% 
  extract_fit_parsnip() %>%
  pluck("fit")
    

plot(all_lassos, xvar = "lambda", label = TRUE, col = rainbow(20))








Code# getting all the cofficients

rownames(all_lassos$beta)
##  [1] "danceability"     "energy"           "loudness"         "speechiness"     
##  [5] "acousticness"     "instrumentalness" "liveness"         "valence"         
##  [9] "tempo"            "duration_ms"      "genre_latin"      "genre_pop"       
## [13] "genre_r.b"        "genre_rap"        "genre_rock"



Code
lasso_coefs <- all_lassos$beta  %>% 
  as.matrix() %>%  
  t() %>% 
  as.data.frame() %>% 
  mutate(lambda = all_lassos$lambda ) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = -lambda, 
               names_to = "term", 
               values_to = "coef")

lasso_coefs %>% filter(coef != 0, lambda > 1)
## # A tibble: 40 × 3
##    lambda term          coef
##     <dbl> <chr>        <dbl>
##  1   5.17 genre_pop    1.26 
##  2   4.71 genre_pop    2.40 
##  3   4.29 genre_pop    3.45 
##  4   3.91 genre_pop    4.40 
##  5   3.56 danceability 0.945
##  6   3.56 genre_pop    5.26 
##  7   3.25 danceability 2.94 
##  8   3.25 genre_pop    6.03 
##  9   2.96 danceability 4.77 
## 10   2.96 genre_pop    6.74 
## # ℹ 30 more rows



Code# plotting the journey of each coffiecients shrinkage --- to understand strongest predictors.
lasso_coefs %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = lambda, y = coef, color = term)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_text(data = lasso_coefs %>% filter(lambda == min(lambda)), aes(x = 0.001, label = term), size = 2) + 
  scale_x_log10(limits = c(-2, 2)) +
  guides(color = "none")







Looking at the lambda vs coeff plot, I can see that coefficients are shrking to zero as lambda increases.My lambda is approximately 0.8, which I think fairly takes into account strongest predictors along with other staying/non-penalized predictors. 0.8 is not too big to penalize everything or not too small to not penalize any predictor. The final model I chose simplifies it so much and avoids overfiting and complicating the model overall reducing predictors and computational intensity.
Part d
I think,looking at the lambda vs coeff plot, Interestingly, energy, speechiness, genre_pop and danceability stay without getting penalize (staying non-zero/not removed) till the very last. Similarly, other predictors such as genre_rap and instrumentalness also stayed for quite long. Except these predictors, others got penalized(become zero/ removed) as they shruck faster. This shows that energy, speechiness, genre_pop and danceability are very strong predictors for popularity score of a song follwowed by instrumentalness and genre_rap.

title: Predicting song popularity based acoustic properties
text:
4: finalizing our analysis
Part a
As per the executive’s goal of a simpler model due to shortage in data team, I’d choose the LASSO model beacuse it’s simpler yet not significantly worse, involves less variables which automatically implies less computaional power reducing lot of work which alighns perfectly well if you don’t have data team to manage. On ther other hand, least squares does not penalize any predictor, it may also over-fitt and also is more complex due to using all 16 predictor variables. Since, it’s small exceutive with no data team and prefer simpler model, then we are trading little error the difference between our most parsimonious model and least squares is 12.46-12.16, is 0.20 and it’s 0.2% in the scale of 0-120 and if we also include error bars, it would most probably be off by 1 or 2 point maximum below or above least squares best model.
Part b

Code# Supporting evidence that my lasso model is pretty accurate to least square

# Lets say a new son released and it has these values 
new_song_data <- data.frame(
  valence = 0.75,
  tempo = 120.0,
  duration_ms = 215000,
  popularity = 85,         
  genre = "pop",
  danceability = 0.70,
  energy = 0.68,
  loudness = -5.5,
  speechiness = 0.065,
  acousticness = 0.19,
  instrumentalness = 0.001,
  liveness = 0.11
)



Code# LS prediction

lm_spec <- linear_reg() %>% 
  set_mode("regression") %>% 
  set_engine("lm")

# we specified variable recipe earlier 


ls_workflow <- workflow() %>%
  add_model(lm_spec) %>%
  add_recipe(variable_recipe) 

ls_model <- ls_workflow %>% 
  fit(data = music_sub) 



predict(ls_model, new_data = new_song_data)
## # A tibble: 1 × 1
##   .pred
##   <dbl>
## 1  66.5



Code
predict(final_lasso_model, new_data = new_song_data)
## # A tibble: 1 × 1
##   .pred
##   <dbl>
## 1  64.9


Since the least square model gave 66.5 and lasso gave 64.9, the difference is just 1.6 points which is pretty close and within ranges. This proves the lasso is indeed very accurate as well(of course not exactly accurate) with few variables and simple model.
Part c
Dear Executive, as per our simple yet incredibly effective Lasso Model, these are my two suggestions with regards to increasing or decreaing the popularity of a song.
1.To increase the popualrity of a song, please focus more on improving/ bettering/ working on these top features of a song : danceability, energy, loudness, speechiness, instrumentalness, genre_pop, genre_rap.
2.To decrease the popularity of a song, you can work on valence, tempo, acoustics, genre_r.b,duration_ms, genre_latin,genre_rock.

title: Forecasting 3 PM Temperatures Across Six Australian Cities
text:
Data Context
Daily weather observations from multiple locations around Australia, obtained from the Australian Commonwealth Bureau of Meteorology and processed to create this realtively large sample dataset for illustrating analytics, data mining, and data science using R and Rattle.The data has been processed to provide a target variable RainTomorrow (whether there is rain on the following day - No/Yes) and a risk variable RISK_MM (how much rain recorded in millimeters). Various transformations are performed on the data.The weatherAUS dataset is regularly updated an updates of this package usually correspond to updates to this dataset. The data is updated from the Bureau of Meteorology web site.The locationsAUS dataset records the location of each weather station.The source dataset comes from the Australian Commonwealth Bureau of Meteorology. The Bureau provided permission to use the data with the Bureau of Meteorology acknowledged as the source of the data, as per email from Cathy Toby (C.Toby@bom.gov.au) of the Climate Information Services of the National CLimate Centre, 17 Dec 2008.
You can download the CSV here for analysis.
The weatherAUS dataset is a data frame containing over 140,000 daily observations from over 45 Australian weather stations. Variables include :
Author(s) Graham.Williams@togaware.com
Source Observations were drawn from numerous weather stations. The daily observations are available from https://www.bom.gov.au/climate/data. Copyright Commonwealth of Australia 2010, Bureau of Meteorology.
Definitions adapted from https://www.bom.gov.au/climate/dwo/IDCJDW0000.shtml
References Package home page: https://rattle.togaware.com. Data source: https://www.bom.gov.au/climate/dwo/ and https://www.bom.gov.au/climate/data.

title: Forecasting 3 PM Temperatures Across Six Australian Cities
text:
Setup
Loading packages and preping data

Codelibrary(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(rattle)

data("weatherAUS")
glimpse(weatherAUS)
## Rows: 208,495
## Columns: 24
## $ Date          <date> 2008-12-01, 2008-12-02, 2008-12-03, 2008-12-04, 2008-12…
## $ Location      <chr> "Albury", "Albury", "Albury", "Albury", "Albury", "Albur…
## $ MinTemp       <dbl> 13.4, 7.4, 12.9, 9.2, 17.5, 14.6, 14.3, 7.7, 9.7, 13.1, …
## $ MaxTemp       <dbl> 22.9, 25.1, 25.7, 28.0, 32.3, 29.7, 25.0, 26.7, 31.9, 30…

title: Forecasting 3 PM Temperatures Across Six Australian Cities
text:
Data wrangling and Visualization
filtering 6 rows namely : Hobart, Adelaide, Canberra, Brisbane, Melbourne, and Sydney. Mutating(in this case writing over) temp9am values to be farenheit and then selecting the relevant 6 columns

Code
weather_data <-weatherAUS %>% 
  filter(Location %in% c("Hobart", "Adelaide", "Canberra", "Brisbane", "Melbourne", "Sydney") ) %>% 
  mutate(Temp9am = Temp9am *1.8 + 32, Temp3pm = Temp3pm * 1.8 + 32) %>% 
  select(Temp3pm, Location, WindSpeed9am, Humidity9am, Pressure9am, 
      Temp9am)
  



Code# Checking it out
dim(weather_data)
## [1] 26828     6
head(weather_data)
## # A tibble: 6 × 6
##   Temp3pm Location WindSpeed9am Humidity9am Pressure9am Temp9am
##     <dbl> <chr>           <dbl>       <int>       <dbl>   <dbl>
## 1    69.6 Sydney             17          92       1018.    69.3
## 2    76.6 Sydney              9          83       1018.    72.3
## 3    73.4 Sydney             17          88       1017.    74.3
## 4    69.6 Sydney             22          83       1014.    70.5
## 5    77.9 Sydney             11          88       1008.    72.5
## 6    78.8 Sydney              9          69       1003.    74.8



Code# Arranging it in desending order and then looking at top 3 using head function proving 3 as an argument
top_3_hottest <- weather_data %>% 
  arrange(desc(Temp3pm)) %>% 
  head(3)



Code# checking it out 
top_3_hottest
## # A tibble: 3 × 6
##   Temp3pm Location  WindSpeed9am Humidity9am Pressure9am Temp9am
##     <dbl> <chr>            <dbl>       <int>       <dbl>   <dbl>
## 1    117. Adelaide            13          14       1008.    96.4
## 2    114. Melbourne           54          23       1003.    91.6
## 3    112. Sydney              13          62       1003.    84.0



Code# group_by() makes mini groups of every location and then takes mean of the group  based on temp3pm
temp3pm_6locs <- weather_data %>% 
  group_by(Location) %>% 
  summarise(mean(Temp3pm, na.rm = TRUE))
  



Code# lets check it out 
temp3pm_6locs
## # A tibble: 6 × 2
##   Location  `mean(Temp3pm, na.rm = TRUE)`
##   <chr>                             <dbl>
## 1 Adelaide                           70.8
## 2 Brisbane                           76.7
## 3 Canberra                           67.0
## 4 Hobart                             61.2
## 5 Melbourne                          66.6
## 6 Sydney                             70.9



Code# Density plot of temp3p for  6 locations
ggplot(weather_data, aes(x = Temp3pm, fill = Location)) + 
  geom_density(alpha = 0.6) # alpha adds translucency to see overlap








Code# creating subplot for each city
# facet_wrap() -- basically splits one plot into smaller sub plots based on similar values in a column 
ggplot(weather_data, aes(x = Temp9am, y = Temp3pm, color = Humidity9am)) + geom_point() + facet_wrap(~Location) +
scale_color_gradient(low = "#132B43", high = "#56B1F7")  







Interpreting both the plots.
Interpretation : Part-d (a) — We’re comparing 3pm temperature of the 6 cities and its variability(how much its varying). Brisbane’s afternoons seems to be in general little hotter relative to other cities as its skewed towards right, higher temp. Similarly Canberra’s afternoons seems pretty cool relative to other cities as its skewed towards left. Apart from the extremes, Hobart, Adeliade and Melbourne seems to have overlap and similar temps more skewed towards cold and sydney seems to have most mid-range temperature of them all.
Interpretation : Part-d (b) — In this facet’s scatter plot, we’re comparing humidity of 9 am for different cities. We can see that Adelaide show’s linearly decreasing humidity at 9 am when temperatures of 9am and temperatur of 3pm are hotter. So if morning in Adelaide starts warmer and stays warmer till after, then humidity at 9 am, with certain probablity will be lower. Canberra, Hobart, Melbourne, Canberra and Syndey shows stable higher humidty at 9am, and in all of them at the peak warmer tempertures, humidity seems to drop a bit.

title: Forecasting 3 PM Temperatures Across Six Australian Cities
text:
Mode_1 Building

Code# Specifying the model
lm_spec <- linear_reg() |> 
  set_mode("regression") |> 
  set_engine("lm")

# checking it out
lm_spec
## Linear Regression Model Specification (regression)
## 
## Computational engine: lm



Code# fitting the model
weather_model_1 <-lm_spec |> 
  fit(Temp3pm ~ Temp9am + Location + Pressure9am, data = weather_data)



Code# checking it out 
weather_model_1 |> 
  tidy()
## # A tibble: 8 × 5
##   term               estimate std.error statistic   p.value
##   <chr>                 <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>
## 1 (Intercept)       -146.       5.07      -28.8   9.39e-180
## 2 Temp9am              0.951    0.00404   235.    0        
## 3 LocationBrisbane    -2.39     0.124     -19.3   2.47e- 82
## 4 LocationCanberra     3.53     0.123      28.6   2.37e-177
## 5 LocationHobart      -1.29     0.128     -10.1   3.70e- 24
## 6 LocationMelbourne   -0.0935   0.123      -0.759 4.48e-  1
## 7 LocationSydney      -1.12     0.118      -9.43  4.57e- 21
## 8 Pressure9am          0.154    0.00487    31.8   4.20e-217



Code# Obtaining the predictions + residuals with augment function as it gives both preidctions and residuals for every row
weather_model_1 %>% 
  augment(new_data = weather_data) %>% 
  head(10)
## # A tibble: 10 × 8
##    .pred .resid Temp3pm Location WindSpeed9am Humidity9am Pressure9am Temp9am
##    <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl> <chr>           <dbl>       <int>       <dbl>   <dbl>
##  1  75.9 -6.29     69.6 Sydney             17          92       1018.    69.3
##  2  78.9 -2.22     76.6 Sydney              9          83       1018.    72.3
##  3  80.6 -7.16     73.4 Sydney             17          88       1017.    74.3
##  4  76.6 -6.96     69.6 Sydney             22          83       1014.    70.5
##  5  77.5  0.351    77.9 Sydney             11          88       1008.    72.5
##  6  78.9 -0.108    78.8 Sydney              9          69       1003.    74.8
##  7  74.7 -2.60     72.1 Sydney             15          75        999     71.1
##  8  71.4 -1.41     70.0 Sydney              7          77       1008.    66.0
##  9  68.0 -6.32     61.7 Sydney             19          92       1006.    62.8
## 10  69.4  4.58     73.9 Sydney             11          80       1014     63.0



Code# creating the residual plot for weather model 1 
weather_model_1 %>% 
  augment(new_data = weather_data) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = .pred, y = .resid)) +
  geom_point() + 
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) # coz we want to see where our prediction values fall - below or above 0







It looks like the model is random, I don’t see any particular shape/ pattern like a slope or parabola etc.This shows that the model is correct as it fits the assumptions of Linear regression. The points seem to be heavily scattered in the middle than tails and there seems to some be outliers but not strong enough to make our model incorrect.

Code# getting the metric to evaluate the model's strength
weather_model_1 %>% 
  glance()
## # A tibble: 1 × 12
##   r.squared adj.r.squared sigma statistic p.value    df  logLik     AIC     BIC
##       <dbl>         <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>
## 1     0.757         0.757  5.44    11614.       0     7 -81283. 162584. 162658.
## # ℹ 3 more variables: deviance <dbl>, df.residual <int>, nobs <int>


Interpretaion of the R^2 : The weather_model_1 seems strong as indicated by high R^2 of 0.75687. So the predictor variables – temperature at 9am, Location and pressure at 9am explains approximately 76% of variability in our response varaible – temperature at 3pm. Although it’s not very strong as roughly 24% of variability is still not explained, but in general it seems strong.

Code# cheking the accuracy -- how far my predictions are off 
weather_model_1 %>% 
  augment(new_data = weather_data) %>% 
  summarise(mae = mean(abs(.resid), na.rm = TRUE)) # had to remove the missing values as it was giving mae as na
## # A tibble: 1 × 1
##     mae
##   <dbl>
## 1  4.24


Interpretation of MAE : The mean absolute error is roughly 4, which means that the predictions are off by 4 degrees F for 3pm temperatures. In relative to the scale of the data, which range from 40 degrees F to 120 degress F for 3pm, being 4 degrees F off in range of 80 degrees F (120-40), is 5% (4/80*100). Therefore, the model is 5% off, which means its statistically 95% accourate.
Interpretation of Temp9am and LocationHobart coefficients :
Temp9am coefficient interpretation : When controlling for location and pressure at 9am, we expect 3pm temperatures to roughly increase by 0.95 degree F for every 1 degree F increase in 9am temperature.
LocationHobart interpretation : When controlling for temperature at 9am, pressure at 9 am and other locations, we expect temperature at 3pm in Hobart to be 1.29 degrees F lower than Adelaide on average. ( Adelaide is our reference variable)

text:
Conclusion
So as per the each fold’s mae’s of both weather_model_1 and weather_model_2 shows no overfitting as there’s no extreme fluctuations which shows that both models are generalizing well to unseen data. Comparatively, based on CV metrics, weather_model_2 is better in predicting for 3pm temperatures as it has lower MAE of 4.12 than weather_model_1’s 4.24 MAE and higher R^2 of 0.768 than weather_model_1’s 0.756.
